sectors.name: Banking & financial services
sectors.tagline: Three vetted people for roles where the wrong hire costs more than a quarter.

misses.title: Compliance instinct
misses.label: Invisible on paper
misses.body: Risk appetite and audit mindset can’t be read off a job title. Someone who has never had a control fail on their watch interviews the same as someone who has.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: the incident they were closest to, and what changed afterwards.

misses.title: Domain depth in engineers
misses.label: A generic tech screen misses it
misses.body: Core banking integrations, payment rails, data residency. An excellent backend engineer with none of it will clear a standard interview comfortably.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they had to hold still while everything else moved.

misses.title: Seniority that means something
misses.label: AVP and VP travel badly
misses.body: Titles vary between institutions. A VP at one bank runs a function. At another, they run a spreadsheet. The CV can’t tell you which.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they were accountable for when it went wrong.

misses.title: Speed, because they have offers
misses.label: Slow pipelines lose the good ones
misses.body: Strong BFSI candidates hold two or three offers at once. A four-week process loses them.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: three scored names in about 36 hours, so the clock is yours.

questions.q: Walk me through a control that failed while you owned it.
questions.thin: “We had a reconciliation break. It was escalated and remediated within the window.”
questions.listeningFor: Who found it, how long it ran before anyone did, and what changed so it couldn’t recur. The remediation is the least interesting part of the answer.

questions.q: A core banking system returns stale balances under load. What do you do?
questions.thin: “Add caching and retries, and raise it with the vendor.”
questions.listeningFor: Whether they reach for idempotency and reconciliation before retries, and whether they say out loud that a stale balance is a correctness problem a customer will see.

questions.q: Tell me about a time the regulation and the roadmap disagreed.
questions.thin: “We worked with compliance and found a path forward.”
questions.listeningFor: What was dropped. Somebody lost something in that conversation, and a person who was in it can tell you what and why.

bench: Core banking and payments engineering, 11 yrs

faq.q: Do your experts actually have BFSI backgrounds?
faq.a: Yes. Every interview is run by someone who has worked in the space: people who have managed credit portfolios, built payment infrastructure or led a risk function.

faq.q: Can you cover both business and technology roles?
faq.a: Both. Core banking engineers and data platform leads at one end, risk officers, investment analysts and CFOs at the other. The scorecard changes shape between them. The method stays the same.

faq.q: How do you handle confidential searches?
faq.a: Role details reach only shortlisted candidates, under NDA where you need it. Outreach is discreet by default, because most of the people worth talking to are employed and not looking.

sectors.h1: Where the wrong hire costs more than a quarter.

market.text: people work in India’s 170-plus BFSI capability centres, about one in five of everyone employed in GCCs.
market.source: KPMG in India and Nasscom, BFSI GCCs: The Road Ahead

sectors.name: Enterprise technology
sectors.tagline: Engineering and product people who have actually put something into production and lived with it afterwards.

misses.title: Shipped, or adjacent to shipped
misses.label: A CV cannot tell them apart
misses.body: Everyone on a delivery team appears on the delivery. The person who made the call and the person who attended the meeting write the same bullet point.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they had to give up to ship on the date they shipped.

misses.title: Scale that was inherited
misses.label: Numbers travel without their owners
misses.body: Two million requests a day is a property of the system. It says nothing about the engineer. Plenty of people have worked near large systems without ever having changed one under load.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what broke first, and what they were watching when it did.

misses.title: Architecture opinions with no scar tissue
misses.label: Everyone can name the pattern
misses.body: Reading about event-driven design and having run a double-write migration for six months are different things that interview identically.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: the migration that took longer than planned, and the month it went wrong.

questions.q: Tell me about something you shipped that you would build differently now.
questions.thin: “We would probably pick a different framework.”
questions.listeningFor: What they underestimated, and whether the regret is technical or organisational. Strong answers name a decision. Weak ones name a tool.

questions.q: Walk me through a migration that took longer than planned.
questions.thin: “Scope crept and we had upstream dependencies.”
questions.listeningFor: The double-write period — how long they ran both systems and what they used to decide it was safe to cut over. Anyone who has done one talks about this unprompted.

questions.q: Who disagreed with your architecture, and what happened?
questions.thin: “We aligned on a hybrid approach.”
questions.listeningFor: Whether they can state the other person's case properly. If they cannot put it fairly, they never understood it, and the compromise was just fatigue.

faq.q: Do you cover platform as well as product engineering?
faq.a: Both, and we weight them differently. A platform hire gets systems design and operational ownership weighted higher; a product engineer gets shipping cadence and stakeholder handling. Same six dimensions, different shape.

market.text: people in India’s tech industry after a net 1.35 lakh hires in FY26, on $315 billion of revenue.

sectors.name: Product & SaaS
sectors.tagline: The difference shows in what they killed, what they refused, and what they were wrong about.

misses.title: Judgment, versus process fluency
misses.label: Frameworks are easy to learn
misses.body: RICE, JTBD and a tidy roadmap can all be recited by someone who has never made an unpopular call. The vocabulary is not the skill.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: the feature they argued against that shipped anyway, and what happened next.

misses.title: Ownership of outcomes
misses.label: Everyone launched something
misses.body: A launch is a date. An outcome is what the number did ninety days later, and whether anyone went back to look.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they measured after, and what they did when it disappointed.

misses.title: The ability to say no
misses.label: Roadmaps are full of yes
misses.body: Product judgment shows in refusal far more than in prioritisation. Anyone can rank a backlog; few can tell a large customer no and keep them.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they said to the customer, in the words they used.

questions.q: Tell me about a feature you argued against that shipped anyway.
questions.thin: “I raised my concerns, and the team decided to move forward.”
questions.listeningFor: What happened afterwards — and whether they are willing to say they turned out to be wrong. A product person who has never been wrong in public has not been in enough rooms.

questions.q: What did you kill, and how did you know it was time?
questions.thin: “We sunset a feature with low usage.”
questions.listeningFor: The number they looked at, the number they deliberately ignored, and who they had to convince. Killing things is a political act before it is an analytical one.

questions.q: Describe something customers asked for that you did not build.
questions.thin: “We prioritised based on impact and effort.”
questions.listeningFor: What they actually said to the customer. The refusal is where product taste lives; the roadmap is just its output.

faq.q: Can you assess product sense, or only experience?
faq.a: Product sense is the hardest thing on this list to test and the easiest to fake, which is why we test it with hindsight rather than hypotheticals. Not “how would you prioritise this” — “what did you get wrong, and when did you know”.

market.text: estimated revenue from Indian software products in FY26, up from $21 billion a year earlier.

sectors.name: AI & data
sectors.tagline: Building the model is the easy half. The people worth hiring are the ones who watched it afterwards.

misses.title: Notebooks versus production
misses.label: Both look like machine learning
misses.body: A strong offline result and a system serving real traffic are different disciplines. Many excellent modellers have never owned anything that woke them up at night.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what the model did in production that it never did in evaluation.

misses.title: Data quality, discovered late
misses.label: Everyone says data is messy
misses.body: The useful question is not whether they have seen bad data. It is how they found out, and how long it had been wrong before anyone noticed.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: how they detected it, before how they fixed it.

misses.title: Knowing when not to ship
misses.label: Model metrics are not a decision
misses.body: An F1 score is not a business threshold. People who have shipped ML into a real process can tell you the number the business cared about and who set it.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a model they decided was not worth shipping.

questions.q: What did the model do in production that it never did in evaluation?
questions.thin: “We saw some drift and retrained on fresher data.”
questions.listeningFor: What they were monitoring before it happened, and whether the threshold was set in advance or discovered through a complaint. The monitoring is the answer; the retrain is housekeeping.

questions.q: Tell me about a data quality problem you found late.
questions.thin: “We had an upstream schema change that broke a pipeline.”
questions.listeningFor: How they found it, and what they changed so that class of problem surfaced sooner next time. Anyone can fix a break; few close the detection gap.

questions.q: When did you decide a model was not worth shipping?
questions.thin: “The metrics were not strong enough.”
questions.listeningFor: The business threshold and who set it. People who have only worked offline quote model metrics; people who have shipped quote the number someone else cared about.

faq.q: How do you assess research versus applied roles?
faq.a: Differently, and we say which at intake. Research weighting leans on depth and written reasoning; applied leans on production ownership and measurement. Hiring one against the other's bar is the most common mistake we see in this space.

sectors.h1: We hire on whether they measured it after it shipped.

market.text: AI job openings expected in India by 2027, against a talent pool of about 1.2 million.

sectors.name: Cybersecurity
sectors.tagline: Certificates are a floor. What matters is what they did in the first twenty minutes.

misses.title: Certifications versus incidents
misses.label: One is much easier to acquire
misses.body: A wall of acronyms tells you someone can pass an exam. It tells you nothing about how they behave at two in the morning with an unclear blast radius.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: the last bridge call they were actually on.

misses.title: Risk decisions
misses.label: Everyone maintains a register
misses.body: Security work is a budget problem before it is a technical one. The real signal is what they chose to leave unprotected and how they defended that.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they left unpatched, and who signed the risk off.

misses.title: Removing controls
misses.label: Adding is always safe
misses.body: Anyone can propose more controls. Knowing which ones no longer earn their operational cost requires having actually run them.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a control they took away, and what it had been protecting against.

questions.q: Walk me through the last incident you were on the bridge for.
questions.thin: “We followed the incident response playbook and contained it.”
questions.listeningFor: What time they got the call, what they did in the first twenty minutes, and what they got wrong. This is the question certifications do not survive.

questions.q: What did you have to leave unpatched, and how did you decide?
questions.thin: “We prioritised remediation by CVSS score.”
questions.listeningFor: The compensating control and the name of the person who accepted the residual risk. Security maturity is visible in how comfortably they discuss what they chose not to fix.

questions.q: Tell me about a control you removed.
questions.thin: “We streamlined some legacy processes.”
questions.listeningFor: What it was protecting against and why that changed. People who have only ever added controls have never had to operate them at 3am.

faq.q: Do you cover both technical and governance roles?
faq.a: Yes, and they are almost opposite shapes. A detection engineer is weighted on incident behaviour and systems depth; a GRC lead on documentation, stakeholder handling and regulatory judgment. Running one against the other's rubric is how good people get rejected.

sectors.h1: We hire on the incident they owned.

market.text: people short in India’s cybersecurity workforce in 2024, a gap that grew 35.9% in a year.

sectors.name: Healthcare & life sciences
sectors.tagline: Clinical, regulatory and commercial, and the ability to hold all three when they disagree.

misses.title: Regulatory judgment
misses.label: Guidance is public
misses.body: Anyone can quote the guidance. The people worth hiring are the ones who have had to act where the guidance genuinely did not say.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a decision made in an ambiguity, and what they recommended before escalating.

misses.title: Documentation as a discipline
misses.label: Everyone claims to be rigorous
misses.body: In this sector the record is the work. What was written down, when, and by whom is the difference between a finding and a citation.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a deviation they handled, and how quickly it was documented.

misses.title: The patient, at speed
misses.label: Timelines and evidence disagree often
misses.body: Commercial pressure is real and constant. The question is what they were prepared to lose to hold a position.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what happened when the clinical evidence and the launch date pulled apart.

questions.q: Describe a time the clinical evidence and the timeline disagreed.
questions.thin: “We escalated it to the steering committee for a decision.”
questions.listeningFor: What they recommended before the escalation. Judgment lives in the position they took before passing it upward.

questions.q: What went into a submission that you were uncomfortable with?
questions.thin: “Everything we submitted was compliant with the applicable guidance.”
questions.listeningFor: Whether they can name one genuine ambiguity. Nobody who has actually worked in this space believes the guidance covers everything.

questions.q: Tell me about a protocol deviation you handled.
questions.thin: “It was documented and reported in line with our SOP.”
questions.listeningFor: What the impact assessment concluded and who they told first. The sequence of those two things says a great deal about how they operate.

faq.q: Do you hire for regulated roles outside India?
faq.a: Yes. We run mandates for teams hiring into India and for India-based teams hiring into other jurisdictions. Where the regulatory regime differs, the interviewer differs — we do not assess EU MDR experience with someone who has only worked to CDSCO.

sectors.h1: We hire on judgment when the guidance runs out.

market.text: hospital beds India needs to add by 2047, with targets of 5 million doctors and 12.5 to 15 million nurses.

sectors.name: Pharmaceutical
sectors.tagline: Precision is the whole job, and precision under uncertainty is the part that cannot be taught quickly.

misses.title: Behaviour in the interval
misses.label: Before the cause was known
misses.body: Every investigation eventually finds a cause. What separates people is what they did in the days before anyone knew what they were looking at.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a result they could not explain, and what they did that week.

misses.title: Comfort with an inconclusive close
misses.label: Phase one closes a lot of investigations
misses.body: Some people are entirely comfortable with that and some are not. The uncomfortable ones are usually the ones who have seen it come back.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: an OOS investigation that closed early, and whether they were happy with it.

misses.title: Pushback with something at stake
misses.label: Everyone says they raised concerns
misses.body: Raising a concern in an email is not the same as holding a position that costs you something. The second one is rarer and much more useful.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a timeline they pushed back on, and what it cost them.

questions.q: Tell me about a result you could not explain.
questions.thin: “We investigated and traced it to an assay issue.”
questions.listeningFor: What they did in the interval before the cause was known — stopped, flagged, or carried on. The interval is the answer; the root cause is just the ending.

questions.q: Describe an out-of-specification investigation you led.
questions.thin: “We followed the two-phase process and it closed at phase one.”
questions.listeningFor: Whether they were comfortable with that close, and why. Most people who have run several are not entirely comfortable, and can tell you precisely why not.

questions.q: When did you push back on a timeline?
questions.thin: “I raised it with the programme lead and we adjusted.”
questions.listeningFor: What they were prepared to lose. A pushback with nothing at stake is just a note in a meeting.

faq.q: How do you handle mandates that need site-specific experience?
faq.a: We say so at intake if the pool is genuinely thin, rather than sending three people who are close. Sterile fill-finish and oral solids are not interchangeable, and pretending otherwise wastes a month of your time and ours.

sectors.h1: We hire on what they did while the data was still ambiguous.

market.text: largest pharmaceutical industry in the world by volume, with exports of $30.5 billion in 2024–25.

sectors.name: Manufacturing
sectors.tagline: Operations, engineering and quality leaders who have run plants rather than reported on them.

misses.title: Floor time versus plan time
misses.label: Both appear as operations experience
misses.body: Someone who has stood on a line at three in the morning talks about it differently from someone who has managed the schedule for one. The CV cannot separate them.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they changed that the plan did not call for.

misses.title: Escapes, as well as RCAs
misses.label: Everyone has run a root cause analysis
misses.body: The interesting question is how far a defect travelled before it was caught, and what the containment actually cost.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a quality escape that reached a customer.

misses.title: Recovering a shutdown
misses.label: Nothing runs to schedule
misses.body: Planned maintenance always overruns somewhere. The skill is what they chose to cut to bring it back, and who they had to tell.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what overran, and what they dropped to recover.

questions.q: What did you change on the line that the plan did not call for?
questions.thin: “We optimised process flow to improve throughput.”
questions.listeningFor: Who on the floor told them it was wrong, and whether they listened the first time they were told. Most plant improvements start as someone being ignored.

questions.q: Tell me about a quality escape.
questions.thin: “We completed a root cause analysis and implemented corrective actions.”
questions.listeningFor: How far it travelled before it was caught and what containment cost. Everyone runs an RCA; not everyone has had to make the call to a customer.

questions.q: Describe a shutdown you ran.
questions.thin: “We planned it thoroughly and executed to schedule.”
questions.listeningFor: What overran and what they cut to recover. Nothing of that size runs to plan, and the recovery decisions are the whole skill.

faq.q: Do you cover discrete and process manufacturing?
faq.a: Both, with different interviewers. The failure modes are not alike — a batch process person and a discrete assembly person will each struggle with the other's questions, and neither struggle tells you anything useful.

sectors.h1: We hire on time on the floor.

market.text: jobs created under the PLI schemes by December 2025, on ₹2.16 lakh crore of investment.
market.source: Ministry of Commerce and Industry, February 2026

sectors.name: Industrial & engineering
sectors.tagline: Technical depth for work that gets built once and has to be right.

misses.title: Accountability versus involvement
misses.label: Project teams are large
misses.body: Everyone on a capital project can describe the capital project. Far fewer signed something and carried it.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they signed off that they were not entirely sure about.

misses.title: The decision behind the delay
misses.label: Overruns are always explained late
misses.body: External factors are real and are also the easiest available answer. The decision that caused the slip almost always happened months earlier.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: what they would do differently in month two.

misses.title: Change during construction
misses.label: Drawings change; costs move
misses.body: A revision is a document. The interesting part is the commercial conversation that followed and who absorbed it.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a design change mid-build, and how that conversation went.

questions.q: Tell me about a project that overran.
questions.thin: “There were external dependencies and some weather impact.”
questions.listeningFor: The decision they made in month two that they would make differently. Overruns are almost always caused earlier than they are noticed.

questions.q: What did you sign off that you were not entirely sure about?
questions.thin: “Everything went through the formal approval process.”
questions.listeningFor: Whether they can name one. Engineers who have carried real accountability all have an answer, and usually remember it clearly.

questions.q: Describe a design change during construction.
questions.thin: “We issued a revision and updated the drawings.”
questions.listeningFor: What it cost, who ended up paying for it, and how that conversation went. The technical change is rarely the hard part.

faq.q: Can you hire for site-based and EPC roles?
faq.a: Yes. Site postings need a different conversation about mobility and family circumstances, which we have early rather than at offer stage — it is the most common reason otherwise-good processes collapse in week four.

sectors.h1: We hire on the project that overran, and why.

market.text: of public capital expenditure proposed for 2026–27, up 8.9% on the previous year’s estimate.

sectors.name: Global capability centres
sectors.tagline: Built for GCCs scaling in India, where the difference between a delivery centre and a capability centre is decision rights.

misses.title: Decision rights
misses.label: Both look like seniority
misses.body: Someone can run a team of forty and never have owned a decision the parent did not pre-approve. The title is identical either way.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a decision that was genuinely theirs.

misses.title: Working the gap
misses.label: Everyone mentions overlap hours
misses.body: Timezone problems are usually ownership problems wearing a clock. The people worth hiring moved the work rather than adding calls.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a handover that kept failing, and what they changed.

misses.title: Influence without authority
misses.label: Matrix reporting hides a lot
misses.body: In a GCC most of the important work happens across a line the org chart does not show. Stakeholder handling is weighted heavily here for that reason.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: something the parent got wrong about this market, and what changed.

questions.q: Who owned that decision — here or the parent?
questions.thin: “It was a collaborative decision across both teams.”
questions.listeningFor: Whether they can name one decision that was genuinely theirs. GCC seniority is almost entirely a question about decision rights.

questions.q: Tell me about something the parent organisation got wrong about your market.
questions.thin: “There were some cultural differences to work through.”
questions.listeningFor: What they did about it and whether anything actually changed. This is the clearest line between a delivery centre and a capability centre.

questions.q: How did you handle a handover that kept failing?
questions.thin: “We improved documentation and increased overlap hours.”
questions.listeningFor: Whether they moved the work or moved the people. Adding calls is what you do when you cannot move ownership.

faq.q: Do you help with early-stage GCC build-outs?
faq.a: Yes, and the first ten hires are a different exercise from the next hundred. Early build-out weights decision rights and ambiguity tolerance far above domain depth, because the people you hire first will define what the centre is allowed to own.

sectors.h1: We hire on who actually owned the decision.

market.text: global capability centres in India, employing 2.36 million people on about $98.4 billion of revenue in FY26.

sectors.name: Consumer & digital commerce
sectors.tagline: Where speed, judgment and commercial instinct all have to survive in the same person.

misses.title: Taste that can be defended
misses.label: Portfolios all look good
misses.body: Anyone can show you something attractive. Far fewer can tell you why it is right for that customer at that moment without reaching for a conversion number.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: something they shipped and why, in craft terms as well as commercial ones.

misses.title: Failure they can be specific about
misses.label: Everyone learned a lot
misses.body: The useful signal is the assumption that turned out to be wrong and how quickly they found out.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a launch that did not work.

misses.title: The speed trade, made consciously
misses.label: Fast is the default here
misses.body: Everyone in this sector ships quickly. The question is whether they know what it cost and whether they would take the same trade again.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a time speed cost them quality.

questions.q: Show me something you shipped that you are proud of, and tell me why.
questions.thin: “It drove a significant lift in conversion.”
questions.listeningFor: Whether they can talk about the craft as well as the number. Taste that can only be defended with a metric is a report.

questions.q: What did you launch that failed?
questions.thin: “We learned a lot from it and applied it later.”
questions.listeningFor: The specific assumption that was wrong and how quickly they knew. Vagueness here usually means they were not close enough to it.

questions.q: Tell me about a time speed cost you quality.
questions.thin: “We shipped fast and iterated after.”
questions.listeningFor: What broke, who noticed first, and whether they would take the same trade again. The last part is the one that separates judgment from habit.

faq.q: Do you hire for D2C as well as marketplace businesses?
faq.a: Yes, and we weight them differently. Marketplace roles lean on systems thinking and supply liquidity; D2C leans on brand judgment and margin discipline. People are rarely equally strong at both and we would rather say which is which.

sectors.h1: We hire on taste, and whether they can defend it.

market.text: Indians shopped online in 2024, and quick commerce is forecast to grow over 40% a year to 2030.
market.source: Bain & Company, How India Shops Online 2025

sectors.name: Private equity portfolio
sectors.tagline: Value-creation timelines are real and short. Hiring has to move faster than they do.

misses.title: The first ninety days
misses.label: Everyone says they listened
misses.body: Ninety days is a quarter of the thesis. Someone who spent it understanding the business has spent a meaningful part of the hold period not acting.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: something specific and dated that they changed early.

misses.title: Deciding without enough
misses.label: Information never arrives in time
misses.body: Portfolio operating roles are a sequence of decisions made on partial information. Speed is either a developed skill or it is recklessness, and the two interview similarly.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: a decision made early, and what they would have needed to be sure.

misses.title: Disagreeing with the sponsor
misses.label: Alignment is the usual answer
misses.body: Operators who have never pushed back on a board have not been properly tested. The useful signal is what they protected and how it went.
misses.tell: Where it shows up: something the sponsor wanted that they resisted.

questions.q: What did you change in your first ninety days?
questions.thin: “I spent the time understanding the business and building relationships.”
questions.listeningFor: Something specific and dated. Ninety days is a quarter of the thesis, and a full quarter of listening is a decision in itself.

questions.q: Tell me about a decision you made without enough information.
questions.thin: “I gathered what input I could and made a judgment call.”
questions.listeningFor: What they would have needed to be certain, and why they did not wait for it. That gap is where speed either becomes a skill or becomes luck.

questions.q: What did the sponsor want that you pushed back on?
questions.thin: “We aligned on priorities pretty quickly.”
questions.listeningFor: The thing they protected. Operators who have never disagreed with a board have not been in a hard enough room yet.

faq.q: How fast can you actually move on a portfolio mandate?
faq.a: First three names inside 36 hours of a confirmed brief, and we hold that in this sector specifically because the hold period does not pause while a search runs. What we will not do is send three people faster by lowering the bar — that is the failure mode this whole model exists to avoid.

sectors.h1: We hire on decision speed under a value-creation clock.

common_faq.q: How fast is the first shortlist?
common_faq.a: Three scored candidates in about 36 hours from a confirmed brief. Sourcing, interviews and scoring all happen inside that window.
